name: Clarksville, TN
spotsNotice: All coordinates are APPROXIMATE. Verify access, parking, posted rules and property lines before visiting. Fishing in Tennessee requires a TWRA license for anglers 13 and older.

regulations.summary: Anglers 13 and older need a Tennessee fishing license. Size limits, daily creel limits and seasons differ by species and by water body, and they change, so read the current TWRA Fishing Guide every year.

links.label: Buy a license: Go Outdoors Tennessee

tips: Keep your license on you (the TWRA On The Go / Go Outdoors TN app can store it on your phone).
Tennessee usually holds a Free Fishing Day in early June when no license is needed. Check TWRA for the date.
Military members stationed at Fort Campbell: ask TWRA about resident license eligibility. Fishing on post needs separate Fort Campbell permits.

advisories.summary: Clarksville itself has few direct stream restrictions on the state's main posted list, but parts of the Cumberland River system do carry advisories. Check the current TDEC list before you keep fish to eat.

items.title: Cheatham Reservoir (Cumberland River, upstream of Clarksville)
items.detail: Precautionary advisory for PCBs in certain catfish and black bass (largemouth, smallmouth, spotted). Children, pregnant or nursing women, and women who may become pregnant should not eat these fish from this section; everyone else should limit how often they eat them.

items.title: Some urban creeks and streams
items.detail: Certain urban streams in Tennessee are posted for bacteria (E. coli) after sewer overflows and runoff. Avoid swimming or wading there, don't eat fish from posted streams, and wash your hands before eating.

items.title: After heavy rain
items.detail: Runoff raises bacteria levels for a day or two in any waterway. Wash hands and gear, and cover cuts.

bankSafety: Don't wade in the Cumberland: currents are strong and the bottom drops off suddenly. Watch for barge wakes.
Below dams, water can rise fast when generators start. Horns or sirens mean move to high ground.

spots.name: Liberty Park
spots.description: City park on the Cumberland River beside Clarksville Marina, with paved paths, a pond and open bank. Easy parking and restrooms make it a great first trip.
spots.beginnerTip: Start with a Trout Magnet under a float or a small piece of worm on the Aberdeen #8 hook near any structure (docks, rocks, fallen trees). Stay off the marina docks unless signage allows fishing.

spots.name: McGregor Park & RiverWalk
spots.description: Downtown riverfront park with a long walkway along the Cumberland and a public boat ramp. Lots of rock bank and current breaks.
spots.beginnerTip: Look for slack water behind rocks or bridge pilings: fish rest there out of the current. Bring the bank rod holders and soak bait for catfish in the evening.

photos.caption: The American Queen riverboat at the Clarksville riverfront

spots.name: Red River mouth (near Fort Defiance)
spots.description: Where the Red River meets the Cumberland. Confluences mix current and food, which attracts predator fish. Bank access is limited; scout first.
spots.beginnerTip: Cast a spinnerbait across the current seam (the line where fast and slow water meet) and reel steadily. Don't wade: river bottoms drop off suddenly.

photos.caption: View from Fort Defiance over the confluence

spots.name: Dunbar Cave State Park (Swan Lake)
spots.description: State park with a small lake in front of the cave entrance. Calm water and easy walking: very beginner friendly. Follow state park rules and hours.
spots.beginnerTip: Calm water is perfect for practicing casting. Try a weightless Senko near weed edges for bass and let it sink slowly.

photos.caption: Swan Lake in front of the Dunbar Cave entrance

spots.name: Red River (north Clarksville)
spots.description: Smaller, slower river than the Cumberland with wooded banks. Good for sunfish and bass around fallen trees. Confirm public access before fishing.
spots.beginnerTip: Fallen trees (laydowns) hold fish. Cast parallel to the log rather than over it to avoid snags.

spots.name: Port Royal State Historic Park
spots.description: Historic park where Sulphur Fork Creek meets the Red River, about 20 minutes east of downtown. Quiet banks and shade.
spots.beginnerTip: In creeks, fish the deeper pools below riffles (shallow rippling water). Small spinners and Trout Magnets drifted through pools work well.

spots.name: West Fork Red River
spots.description: Creek running through north Clarksville toward Fort Campbell. Small water, light tackle. Many banks are private: only fish where access is clearly public.
spots.beginnerTip: Walk quietly and keep your shadow off the water. Creek fish spook easily.

spots.name: Yellow Creek at Ellis Mills
spots.description: Rural creek southwest of Clarksville near the Houston County line, about 35 minutes away. Clear pools in summer. Access is mostly at road crossings; respect private land.
spots.beginnerTip: Clear water means fish can see your line: 8 lb mono is great here. Use natural colors like the green pumpkin Senko.

spots.name: Cumberland River at Seven Mile Ferry Rd
spots.description: Public boat ramp on the Cumberland south of downtown, with some bank access around it. Barge traffic and current: keep kids and gear back from the edge, and stay clear of boats launching.
spots.beginnerTip: Use enough sinker weight to hold bottom in the current (add a sliding egg sinker above a swivel). Put the rod in the bank holder and watch the tip.

spots.name: Cheatham Dam tailwater (upstream)
spots.description: Popular Army Corps of Engineers tailwater about 35 minutes upstream. Strong, sudden currents when turbines run. Cheatham Reservoir carries PCB consumption advisories for certain catfish and black bass, so check TDEC guidance before keeping fish.
spots.beginnerTip: Stay behind railings and out of restricted zones. Sirens and horns mean water releases. Great place to watch experienced anglers and learn.
spots.advisory: PCB advisory area: see Safety page.
